title: Ophthalmology and Otorhinolaryngology
description: Eye examination, causes of blindness in Nigeria, the red eye, cataract, glaucoma, ear disease and hearing loss, nose and throat conditions, and ENT emergencies.

topics.title: Eye Examination and Blindness in Nigeria
topics.summary: Visual acuity, eye examination, causes of blindness and visual impairment, and VISION 2020.

notes.b: Visual acuity is measured with a Snellen chart at 6 metres (normal 6/6); use a pinhole to correct refractive error; count fingers, hand movements and light perception for very poor vision; illiterate E charts or picture charts for children and non-readers. Examination includes eyelids, conjunctiva, cornea (fluorescein for abrasions and ulcers), anterior chamber, pupils (direct and consensual reflexes; relative afferent pupillary defect — optic nerve disease), lens (red reflex), intraocular pressure (tonometry — normal 10–21 mmHg), fundoscopy (optic disc cup:disc ratio, retina, vessels), eye movements and visual fields. WHO categories: moderate visual impairment (< 6/18 to 6/60), severe (< 6/60 to 3/60), blindness (< 3/60 in the better eye).

The Nigeria National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey (2005–2007) found about 4.2% blindness among adults aged 40+ (over a million blind people). Leading causes: cataract (about 43% of blindness — treatable), glaucoma (about 17%, irreversible; primary open-angle glaucoma is common, early-onset and severe in Africans), uncorrected refractive error (leading cause of visual impairment), corneal opacity (trachoma, onchocerciasis, measles and vitamin A deficiency, harmful traditional eye medicines), and posterior segment disease (diabetic retinopathy, AMD). About 80% of blindness is avoidable. VISION 2020: The Right to Sight (WHO/IAPB) prioritised cataract, refractive error, trachoma (SAFE strategy — Surgery, Antibiotics (azithromycin), Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement), onchocerciasis (ivermectin) and childhood blindness. Eye care services remain concentrated in cities.

topics.title: The Red Eye, Cataract and Glaucoma
topics.summary: Conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis, acute glaucoma, eye injuries, cataract and chronic glaucoma.

notes.b: Conjunctivitis: bacterial (purulent discharge — topical antibiotics), viral (watery, follicles, highly contagious — 'Apollo' epidemic haemorrhagic conjunctivitis in Nigeria; hygiene), allergic (itching, seasonal — vernal keratoconjunctivitis common in African children), and ophthalmia neonatorum (gonococcal or chlamydial — within the first month; prevented with tetracycline eye ointment at birth). Danger signs in a red eye (refer urgently): reduced vision, severe pain, photophobia, circumcorneal (ciliary) injection, abnormal pupil, corneal opacity or staining, and raised IOP. Keratitis/corneal ulcer (bacterial, fungal — after vegetable-matter trauma in farmers; herpes simplex — dendritic ulcer; never give steroids) and harmful traditional eye medicines are major causes of corneal blindness. Anterior uveitis (pain, photophobia, small irregular pupil, ciliary flush — steroids and mydriatics). Acute angle-closure glaucoma (sudden painful red eye, hazy cornea, mid-dilated fixed pupil, very high IOP, nausea, halos — emergency: acetazolamide, pilocarpine, timolol, then laser iridotomy). Eye injuries: chemical burns — immediate copious irrigation; penetrating injuries — shield, no pressure, urgent referral.
k: Fungal keratitis in farmers; no steroids

notes.b: Cataract is opacification of the lens — age-related (most common), congenital (rubella, galactosaemia), traumatic, diabetic, steroid-induced; presents with gradual painless blurring, glare and loss of red reflex. Treatment is surgery: manual small-incision cataract surgery (MSICS — high-quality, low-cost and widely used in Nigeria) or phacoemulsification, with intraocular lens implantation. Couching (traditional displacement of the lens into the vitreous) still occurs and causes blindness. Primary open-angle glaucoma: asymptomatic, progressive optic neuropathy with enlarged cup:disc ratio (> 0.6 or asymmetry) and peripheral visual field loss (tunnel vision) — often presents late in Nigeria with advanced damage; risk factors: African ancestry, age, family history, high IOP, myopia. Treatment: topical drugs (prostaglandin analogues — latanoprost; beta-blockers — timolol; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; alpha-agonists), laser trabeculoplasty and trabeculectomy surgery. Lifelong adherence and screening of first-degree relatives are important.

topics.title: Retina, Childhood Eye Disease and Refractive Error
topics.summary: Diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, childhood blindness, refractive errors and low vision.

notes.b: Diabetic retinopathy: non-proliferative (microaneurysms, dot-and-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots), proliferative (new vessels — vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment) and maculopathy (commonest cause of visual loss in diabetes). Screening at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and annually; treat with glycaemic and BP control, laser photocoagulation and anti-VEGF injections. Hypertensive retinopathy: arteriolar narrowing, AV nipping, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and papilloedema (malignant hypertension). Sickle cell retinopathy (especially HbSC — 'sea-fan' neovascularisation). Retinal detachment: floaters, flashes and a curtain over vision — urgent surgery. Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden painless loss of vision, cherry-red spot. Papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure.
k: Maculopathy: main cause of visual loss

notes.b: Childhood blindness in Nigeria is caused by corneal scarring (measles, vitamin A deficiency — xerophthalmia with night blindness, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia; harmful traditional eye medicines), congenital cataract (needs early surgery to prevent amblyopia), congenital glaucoma (large hazy corneas — buphthalmos), retinopathy of prematurity (increasing with neonatal care — screen preterm babies), retinoblastoma (leukocoria, squint — urgent referral) and cortical visual impairment. Amblyopia ('lazy eye') from squint, refractive error or deprivation must be treated before about 7–8 years (glasses, patching). Refractive errors: myopia (short-sightedness — concave lenses), hypermetropia (long-sightedness — convex lenses), astigmatism (cylindrical lenses) and presbyopia (age-related loss of near focus after about 40 — reading glasses). School eye screening and affordable spectacles address refractive error. Low-vision services help those with irreversible loss.

topics.title: Ear Disease and Hearing Loss
topics.summary: Otitis media and externa, chronic suppurative otitis media, hearing loss and its causes.

notes.b: Acute otitis media (young children; ear pain, fever, bulging red tympanic membrane; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella): analgesia and amoxicillin. Otitis media with effusion ('glue ear'): hearing loss without acute infection — watchful waiting, grommets if persistent. Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM — common in Nigerian children, linked to poverty, crowding and malnutrition): persistent ear discharge through a tympanic membrane perforation for > 2 weeks; treatment by aural toilet (dry mopping) and topical quinolone drops (ciprofloxacin); cholesteatoma (attic perforation, foul discharge, can erode bone) needs mastoid surgery. Complications of otitis media: mastoiditis (post-auricular swelling pushing the ear forwards), facial nerve palsy, meningitis, brain abscess and lateral sinus thrombosis. Otitis externa (swimmers, instrumentation — pain on moving the pinna): cleaning and topical drops; malignant otitis externa in elderly diabetics (Pseudomonas). Foreign bodies and wax impaction are common; avoid inserting objects into ears.

Hearing loss is conductive (external or middle ear — wax, otitis media, perforation, otosclerosis) or sensorineural (cochlea or auditory nerve — presbycusis, noise-induced from generators and factories, ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides — streptomycin, gentamicin, kanamycin in MDR-TB; quinine; cisplatin), meningitis, congenital rubella, CMV, kernicterus, birth asphyxia, Lassa fever (sudden sensorineural deafness in survivors) and genetic causes). Tuning fork tests (512 Hz): Rinne (air conduction > bone conduction normally; negative in conductive loss) and Weber (lateralises to the affected ear in conductive loss, to the better ear in sensorineural loss). Pure tone audiometry, tympanometry, and otoacoustic emissions/ABR for newborn screening. Early detection in infants (universal newborn hearing screening) enables hearing aids, cochlear implants and language development. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an emergency (steroids).

topics.title: Nose, Throat and ENT Emergencies
topics.summary: Epistaxis, sinusitis, tonsillitis, airway emergencies, foreign bodies and head and neck cancers.

notes.b: Epistaxis: most bleeds are anterior from Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) — sit forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes, then cautery or anterior nasal packing; posterior bleeds (elderly, hypertensive) may need posterior packing or surgery; check BP and clotting. Rhinosinusitis (nasal obstruction, discharge, facial pain) — mostly viral; antibiotics if bacterial features persist; allergic rhinitis (intranasal steroids, antihistamines). Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (adolescent boys with recurrent epistaxis and obstruction) are important. Tonsillitis (viral or group A streptococcal — penicillin V for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever); peritonsillar abscess (quinsy — trismus, uvula deviation, 'hot potato' voice — drainage). Adenotonsillar hypertrophy causes snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea in children (adenotonsillectomy). Hoarseness lasting > 3 weeks requires laryngoscopy to exclude laryngeal cancer (smokers).

Stridor indicates upper airway obstruction: in children — croup (laryngotracheobronchitis; barking cough; dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline), epiglottitis (toxic, drooling, tripod position — do not examine the throat; secure the airway in theatre; Hib vaccine has reduced it), diphtheria (grey membrane), and inhaled foreign bodies (sudden choking; groundnuts and small toys; right main bronchus; rigid bronchoscopy); in adults — laryngeal tumours, angioedema, trauma, Ludwig's angina (dental infection spreading to submandibular spaces — airway threat). Foreign bodies in the ear and nose (beads, seeds) are common in children; button batteries in the nose or oesophagus are emergencies. Oesophageal foreign bodies (coins, fish bones) need endoscopic removal. Tracheostomy secures the airway in prolonged obstruction. Head and neck cancers: nasopharyngeal, laryngeal, oral cavity (smoking, alcohol) and Burkitt lymphoma of the jaw in children; a persistent neck lump in an adult requires evaluation (FNAC).
